Players take on the role of a space agency planner, preparing and managing a robotic mission to the Moon. They make key decisions throughout the mission, including selecting a spacecraft, assembling a ground team, choosing scientific instruments, managing the budget, and selecting a rocket, orbit, and launch date. After launch, players operate their spacecraft, respond to unexpected challenges, manage resources, and evaluate their mission through a detailed report.

Through simplified engineering decisions and visible consequences, players learn how factors such as mass, power, communication, and scientific equipment affect a mission's success. By making space exploration approachable and engaging, the game aims to spark curiosity about space science, engineering, and the real-world work behind space missions.
details:
Project Details — DEAD CODERS: SPACE MISSION

DEAD CODERS: SPACE MISSION is a 2D sci-fi space exploration game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It puts players in the role of a space mission planner, allowing them to experience the process of preparing, launching, and operating a robotic mission to the Moon.

The game begins with players making a series of decisions to design their mission. They select a spacecraft, assemble a ground team, choose scientific instruments and payloads, and decide on a suitable rocket, lunar orbit, and launch date. Each decision has consequences: equipment affects the spacecraft's mass, power consumption, storage capacity, and scientific capabilities, while the available budget places limits on what players can bring. Once the mission is ready, players watch a launch sequence before moving on to the spacecraft's operations.

During the mission, players monitor telemetry, manage resources such as battery power and scientific data storage, and respond to unexpected events. The mission eventually concludes with a detailed report showing the player's decisions, mission events, scientific data returned, overall performance, and recommendations for improvement. Reports are saved locally, allowing players to revisit previous attempts and learn from their mistakes.

The main benefit of the project is that it makes the complex subject of spacecraft engineering more accessible. Rather than overwhelming players with technical terminology or complicated simulations, the game introduces important engineering concepts through straightforward choices and visible consequences. For example, players can discover how adding scientific instruments affects spacecraft mass and power requirements, or how communication equipment is necessary to return collected data. Contextual explanations and lessons in the mission report further reinforce these concepts.

Our intended impact is to encourage curiosity about space exploration, science, and engineering, particularly among people who may not otherwise have an opportunity to engage with these subjects. By presenting mission planning as an interactive experience, we hope to help players better appreciate the many considerations involved in real-world space missions.

The project was developed using C++17 and the raylib library, with the C++ standard library used for supporting functionality. We used a modular code structure to organize the different parts of the game, alongside custom visual assets, fonts, sound effects, and interface elements. We also referred to NASA's CubeSat 101: Basic Concepts and Processes for First-Time CubeSat Developers (2017) to inform the game's educational explanations and simplified engineering mechanics.

Creatively, the project combines the structure of a management game with the presentation of a sci-fi space exploration experience. Instead of relying on traditional quizzes or text-heavy educational interfaces, players learn by making decisions, observing their outcomes, and reviewing their mission reports. The visual design uses a futuristic navy, cream, teal, and coral colour palette, with illustrated spacecraft, animated interface elements, telemetry displays, and a paper-style mission dossier.

Throughout development, our team considered several factors: educational value, accessibility, gameplay simplicity, and technical accuracy. We wanted the game to be engaging without sacrificing its educational purpose, so we simplified certain engineering calculations while retaining the underlying principles. We also made a distinction between real engineering concepts and fictional gameplay values, such as simplified spacecraft prices and mission statistics. Finally, we considered usability and presentation, ensuring that players could understand their options, track their budget, and see how their decisions affected the mission without needing prior knowledge of aerospace engineering.
